a stochastic control problem, in which the optimal cost function satisfies a variationally constrained generalized Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. The necessary conditions for optimality were initially reported by Sir\'e and Zhang in 2019. Our work builds on these findings, offering a unique variationally constrained minimization problem that is equivalent to solving the generalized HJB equation. We establish the well-posedness of this new problem, confirming the existence and uniqueness of a solution. In contrast to standard stochastic control problems, the generalized GJB equation involves the non-smooth maximum operator, hindering the application of established numerical methods, such as the finite element method in space and Euler-Maruyama discretization in time. In response, we propose a robust finite element discontinuous Galerkin scheme, which effectively handles the non-smoothness of the maximum operator, in conjunction with a corresponding control problem. We also demonstrate the convergence of the proposed method, and conduct numerical experiments to illustrate its performance and practical utility.

Networks (TCNs) have been successfully applied to a wide range of sequence modeling tasks, but their TCN architecture lacks invariance to time shifts, which limits their ability to generalize and requires extensive time synchronization between sensors, especially in complex multi-sensor systems. This research introduces a novel architecture called the Fourier TCN that integrates the Fourier transform into the TCN architecture to enhance its invariance to time shifts. The new architecture was tested on a multivariate time series dataset and compared to the original TCN and other state-of-the-art models like TCN+Repetition and Fourier Networks. The results show that the Fourier TCN consistently surpasses the competing models in terms of prediction accuracy, but it also highlights some numerical stability issues associated with the new architecture.

In this approach, Decoupling strategies that separate object pose prediction into intermediate tasks, such as 3D pose estimation after 2D pose estimation and 6D pose estimation after 3D pose estimation have wide-ranging applications. We explore the fundamental issue that standard regression loss functions may hinder 3D and 6D object pose estimation by addressing the scale ambiguity inherent in intermediate 2D and 3D pose results. This problem becomes evident when considering the standard $L_2$ loss, where the model may opt to predict an average solution instead of accurate instances. To resolve this, we introduce the $L_{2+}$ loss function, which enforces a positive scale constraint to obtain more reliable intermediate 3D pose instances. By using 3D pose as an auxiliary task and pretraining a 2D-to-3D predictor with this loss, we observe a notable 6D pose estimation performance improvement. This method can be seamlessly integrated into existing object pose estimation frameworks, enhancing overall system efficiency.

By utilizing atom parities, we can derive practical information from existing experimental data, which can then be used to place constraints on the strong interaction and improve our understanding of the nuclear force. Our study leverages heavy atom parity measurements to derive new sum rules and makes predictions for the missing parity data, which can then be used to derive a new parity super-virtual state value. With this enhanced input, we can significantly improve the accuracy of the quasi-elastic scattering cross-section calculations, which are essential for understanding the nuclear force. yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) are generated by catalyzing quantum optics processes with single photons, resulting in unique quantum characteristics such as enhanced non-classical effects including increased catalytic states, stronger phase stability, and greater photon anti-bunching. Microwave Background can be explained by the creation of multiple universes. However, this hypothesis falls short because it fails to account for large-scale globular structures. A new proposal suggests that global voids, extensive dark energy-filled spaces, may form due to phase transitions or the creation of multiple universes. These spaces can be created when the boundaries between different universes move and expand faster than the speed of light, causing them to merge. This process can be repeated, resulting in larger and larger spaces. These spaces can be detected by analyzing the Cosmic Microwave Background for distinct signals. These signals may be stronger in directions pointing towards the center of the space. A study of the Cosmic Microwave Background can help determine the properties of dark energy, such as its equation of state.

few-shot learning has been rapidly advancing in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for calculating prototypes often result in misleading prototypes, especially when the training classes are not balanced. In this paper, we question the prevalent practice of using prototypes derived from equal or balanced weights in confusion. By analyzing the impact of prototypes on model performance, we show that these prototypes can act as powerful labels leaking during training. As an alternative, we propose a novel meta-loss function inspired by lossy-Jain indexing that enables models to identify more meaningful prototypes and suppress the influence of misleading ones, achieving significant improvements in performance with minimal confusion.

improving the recommendation performance when item data is limited in a single domain. This project explores a new approach called Multi-domain multi-task contrastive recommendation, which combines contrastive learning with multi-domain multi-task matrix factorization to achieve this goal. This innovative method not only models latent semantic connections between items within and outside the same domain but also introduces a multi-domain contrastive loss function to model these connections. To efficiently contrast user profiles across different domains, we adopted a contrastive structure known as InfoNCE. The proposed method's effectiveness was verified through the use of a real-world dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing baseline methods.

on Deformed Special Relativity, that Fock's coordinate transformation can be developed using a novel, deformed Minkowski spacetime based on a specific deformed commutation relationship between coordinates, which we call FSM. Notably, this framework retains deformed linear transformations between coordinates while yielding standard Special Relativity in the limit as an arbitrary deformation parameter approaches zero. Building on this foundation, we're able to derive standard Riemann Christoffel symbols and a standard metric tensor that produce the standard gravitational field through standard Einstein's gravity equations. Dialysis is used as a temporary treatment, but it has significant drawbacks compared to a kidney transplant.
This research focuses on a more efficient dialysis plan for patients awaiting transplants, aiming to minimize the burden of dialysis while ensuring its continuous provision.
Initially, an optimal scheduling strategy for dialysis was developed to minimize the number of dialysis sessions, avoiding the need for a dedicated dialysis machine for each waiting patient.
This new schedule was formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming problem, ensuring that dialysis machines are not overbooked.
Although an optimal solution was found using a solver, a more practical heuristic algorithm was also developed.
This study applied the new scheduling strategy to data from a university hospital in Japan, demonstrating significant improvements in the number of dialysis machines needed, as well as the number of doctors and nurses required.

interactions between particles and the cosmic microwave background remains largely theoretical, as accelerating particles beyond an energy level of approximately 10^21 electron volts results in significant interactions with the background. This investigation examines the implied connections between the two processes when the cross-section for particle self-interaction reaches its peak, specifically exploring the relationship between the threshold for pair production and the mean free path of the super-heavy particles. Using the established relationship between the two, researchers have determined the critical point at which particle self-interaction exceeds the expansion rate of the universe, finding it to be approximately 10^21 electron volts with protons, 10^19 electron volts with nuclei, and 10^13.5 electron volts with the GZK cutoff. Pyramid Networks (FPN), have achieved significant success in recent years. However, FPN's reliance on merging detector outputs from various feature scales can introduce unnecessary complexity and a risk of background noise. To overcome these challenges and pave the way for more efficient multi-scale detection, this paper introduces the concept of optimal detector selection, in which only the targets that appear on each feature scale are identified and a simpler, streamlined approach is proposed. Building upon this theory, we introduce a novel single-scale detection method based on optimal detector selection, demonstrating that it can match or surpass the performance of multi-scale detectors like FPNR-50/101 and several prominent detectors on PASCAL VOC, in addition to requiring fewer computational resources and a smaller number of proposals. In the context of hard mining-based detection, our single-scale method also demonstrates effectiveness.

Another approach is sparse non-negative matrix factorization (SNMF), which reduces dimensionality while representing both the data points and the reduction basis as sparse matrices. As the number of base station antennas increases, small small interference is expected, allowing for simple system analysis and low complexity precoding methods like transmit beamforming. In this research, we investigate the performance of the effective signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio in the large system limit, considering multi-cell scenarios. Understanding the physical mechanisms responsible for shaping these disks is crucial for interpreting their properties. This study focuses on a specific ISO, IR 21 in the Ophiuchus star-forming region, which exhibits unusual far-infrared brightness variations, suggesting a significant spatial structure. By creating two-dimensional radiative transfer models, we analyze the observed brightness distribution and spectral energy spectrum of IR 21. Our results indicate that the most probable model for IR 21 involves a binary system of gas disks about 2600 AU apart. These disks are tilted at an inclination angle of 45 degrees and consist of dust particles following a power-law size distribution starting from 0.055 micrometers. Although a single disk or other binary configurations were also considered, none matched the observations as closely as the preferred binary disk model. This research emphasizes the importance of combining spatial and spectral data to gain a comprehensive understanding of the physical structure of protoplanetary disks.

we've found that certain types of chemical reactions are consistently followed by a specific pattern of molecule movement, known as convection rolls. This phenomenon occurs in about 15% of reactions and is robust across different reaction scenarios, remaining stable even when the system is significantly enlarged. The formation of convection rolls is caused by the interaction between two opposing forces: the movement of ions due to an electric field and the resistance offered by solvent molecules. These rolls can significantly slow down the increase in viscosity as temperature drops, which in turn affects the timing of reactions in certain chemical systems. Our findings suggest that the physical properties of the surrounding solvent can have a more profound impact on reactions than previously thought, especially in the case of similar molecules with identical structures.

In this research, we utilize high-resolution neutron and X-ray diffraction techniques to investigate the charge transfer dynamics between NCM532 cathode and Al current collector in solid-state batteries, as they are charged and discharged. Our analysis reveals that lattice expansions occur bidirectionally in both x and z axes during charge, in contrast to liquid-state batteries where current limitation leads to unidirectional lattice expansions. Notably, we also discover that the Al current collector plays a crucial role in facilitating a reaction limited charge, leading to lattice expansions at the electrode interface. Furthermore, our research uncovers a previously unobserved phenomenon in solid-state batteries, where the NCM532 grain boundary phase reacts with hydrogen, likely stemming from hydrogen contamination. Our findings offer valuable insights into the complex internal workings of solid-state batteries, thereby contributing to a more refined design and manufacturing process.

By comparing 64Ni6 gamma-ray spectra from recent experiments, we identified a consistent set of gamma-ray transitions formed by a specific nuclear particle model. These particles, occupying f77h8 and f66h9 configurations, create an intrinsic structure with pairs of particles in blocked orbitals. A key feature of this model is that it predicts an absolute minimum state, along with a set of quasi-spin symmetry breaking excitations. This structure is explained by a strong pairing of particles within the blocked f-shell, which is a characteristic of the "island of stability" in nuclear physics. The particle model is also characterized by a strong deformation of the nuclear shape, which is a significant factor in understanding the complex behavior of nickel-64. The irreps of SU3, which are used to describe the collective motion of nucleons, were found to be a useful tool in identifying the observed particle rotations. The f77h8 and f66h9 configurations were found to be a key factor in understanding the complex behavior of nickel-64, which is a result of the interplay between nucleon-nucleon forces and the nuclear potential. The importance of these configurations in nickel-64 is a key factor in the search for the "island of stability" in nuclear physics.

Sketch has long been utilized in a variety of streaming applications. Its versatility is highlighted by its capacity to be applied in a deterministic manner across diverse data types and metric spaces while preserving efficiency and accuracy. However, count sketch falls short when dealing with high-quality or faulty data streams. To address this challenge, we develop an efficient algorithm that can produce a reliable sketch for points in any metric space, allowing it to be restored to a repeated close approximation of the distance between two long streams of the same dimension and quality. Our algorithm can be restored to a repeated close approximation of the distance between two long streams of identical dimension and quality. Surprisingly, our algorithm achieves this with a deterministic complexity that is only a constant factor above the optimal memory requirement, which does not depend on the dimensionality of the space. CountSketch is effectively used as the core building block of our algorithm. Additionally, we extend our approach to accommodate arbitrary quality factors and provide a common generalization for all cases. These results in deterministic complexity are close to the theoretical lower bounds and are almost matching for any desired quality parameter. Furthermore, our algorithm has a remarkably simple structure consisting of only two components. These advances open up new possibilities for extending CountSketch to more complex and realistic data streaming scenarios.

we studied a specific area in the starburst galaxy Mrk 273, analyzing its neutral gas properties like gas velocity, temperature, and density at both optical and millimeter wavelengths. However, its inherent characteristics, including inherent inaccuracy and incompletion, pose significant challenges to traditional database technologies, necessitating a reevaluation of database management systems' capabilities. The issue of missing or inaccurate data is ubiquitous, and addressing it is crucial for reliable query processing, with impact extending to areas such as resource allocation and query optimization. Our research focuses on assessing the probability of successful joins in concurrent transactions within the Linked Data environment. Concurrent transactions are increasingly common due to the adoption of transactional database systems, and we investigate how to accurately estimate the number of concurrent successful joins, an essential metric for assessing lock contention and query performance in stored-procedure query processing. In order to achieve this, we developed a novel approach that involves analyzing the characteristics of concurrent transactions and their impact on query execution, taking into account the unique properties of Linked Data. Our approach involves an abstract interpretation of the query, leading to more accurate estimation of concurrent successful joins, with results that can inform the development of more efficient stored-procedure query processing techniques. Our approach was experimentally validated and showed a significant improvement in successful query execution time, demonstrating a substantial reduction in lock contention, with outcomes that have implications for the development of more efficient transactional database management systems.

This paper proposes a new optical flow-based non-rigid registration method that incorporates a hyperelastic constitutive model, specifically the Mooney-Rivlin model, into the flow equations. To address this issue, LiDAR point cloud data compression techniques are crucial. Point cloud downsampling methods can be divided into hand-crafted and data-driven approaches. While the latter offers superior performance, most are limited by the need to downsample points individually, which is inefficient. To overcome this limitation, we introduce PointQuatNet, a novel compression framework that employs a multi-layer perceptron to predict feature vectors and unit quaternions from local point neighborhoods. By leveraging the compact and efficient representation of quaternions for rotation, QuatNet achieves 32x faster forward propagation compared to traditional methods. QuatNet's performance has been validated on multiple datasets and demonstrates significant improvements in mean Average Precision and computational efficiency over state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, QuatNet exhibits remarkable downscaling ability, surpassing the 100 MB limit of edge devices, and can be deployed on a Raspberry Pi 4B, making it an efficient and practical solution for LiDAR data compression.

This observed behavior suggests the existence of a mechanism influencing growth guided by contact interactions between growing axons. We have discovered that a specific type of growth cone model, sensitive to contact and guided by it, can account for the rhythmic movement of crossing axons. Our theoretical research suggests that the relationship between axonal growth and the environment in which it occurs can be modeled as a complex adaptive system, characterized by a complex relationship between axonal growth and the surrounding environment.

adzievskii-Paddack effect causes an asymmetric force on Earth's rotating body due to the re-emission of solar energy as thermal radiation. We investigated the YORP effect's impact on Earth's rotation by modeling the planet as a spinning top with two additional degrees of freedom: precession and nutation. We derived the YORP torque formula, considering the terrestrial albedo and infrared emissivity variations, as well as the ocean's influence on the effect. Our results show the YORP torque's magnitude is $10^{-16}$ Nm, which is $10^{-10}$ times smaller than the gravitational torque from the Moon and Sun. Consequently, the YORP effect's influence on precession and nutation periods is negligible, estimated at $10^{-4}$ seconds and $10^{-2}$ seconds, respectively. In contrast, the YORP effect's potential long-term future, over billions of years, may eventually push Earth's rotation into a state of precession resonance with the Moon's orbital resonance.

However, the influence of a stimulus's semantic category on neural activity in ventral temporal cortex remains unclear. Using single-unit neural recordings from macaque VTC while they performed a passive visual task, we found that both neutral and animal-related images had distinct effects on neural activity. We found that images belonging to the animal-related category activated a larger network of neurons in VTC than did images belonging to the neutral-related category, which in turn activated a more localized group of neurons. This difference in network size was more pronounced when comparing images that share semantic features, such as shape and color, rather than those that do not share any features. We also found that images that are similar in meaning activate more overlapping populations of neurons in VTC, especially when they share semantic features. This suggests that both a stimulus's and its surrounding context's semantic features activate hierarchical neural populations in VTC, which may be essential for higher-level cognitive functions.

The concept of taking the product of models has been known for decades, but recent work has redefined this concept using a category-theoretic framework, revealing its limitations in applications. This redefinition has been followed by investigations into the existence of model companions, which has a long history in logical theory. In these re-examinations, a formal proof has been provided for the model companion of S4, showing that it behaves similarly to a variant of the logic with additional modal operators. These re-examinations have a connection through the lens of dual abstract modal logics, which offer a unified approach to studying both model companions and modal logics. This relationship has a co-inductive nature, as the model companion of a logic can itself be analyzed to find its corresponding dual abstract modal logics. This framework has a correspondence with traditional logical systems, such as normal modal logics and S4-like logics with positive introspection. The model companion of a normal modal logic is shown to be equivalent to a positive introspection variant of the original logic. The dual abstract modal logics of positive modal logics are found to be trivial, but non-trivial model companions can be constructed for positive variants of more complex logics, such as the modal logic of tree inclusion.

While numerous theories have been proposed to explain knots in proteins, a significant obstacle persists in validating these proposals due to the scarcity of actual simulation data. This difficulty arises from the extensive computational resources required to simulate large-scale protein movements. Our recent research addresses this gap by applying dynamic modes analysis to examine the structural relationships between knots in pairs of tied proteins during their conformational transitions. By efficiently simulating a broad range of folding pathways, we are able to track the formation of knots at large scales, revealing that these intricate patterns emerge from the interaction between two specific modes of motion in the proteins. This remarkable consistency is corroborated by additional tests, providing an accessible target for further examination by the scientific community.

Unlike traditional methods, D2D communication offers several advantages, including faster data transfer rates, reduced network load, and improved spectrum efficiency. To address these challenges, this work incorporates multiple real-world constraints, including data transfer queue buildup, into an optimization problem. By using the device data and channel information, this research proposes a new, time-average optimal D2D communication policy called Backpressure Optimal Policy (BOP).  It is important to note that the BOP policy is not feasible to implement in practice due to its reliance on both data and channel conditions, and it operates without considering the effects of channel time variation. However, researchers are increasingly interested in exploring other types of symmetric random matrices, such as those with off-diagonal entries that follow various probability distributions. In this paper, we investigate the circular law, which represents the typical distribution of eigenvalues for a specific new class of random matrices. This new class includes but is not limited to matrices with entries following stable distributions in the sense of Levy. The concept of critical slowing down, which occurs near a bifurcation point, has been proven to manifest in various forms of dynamical systems, including the logistic map, Ricker map, and Hassell map. This research further investigates the universality of critical slowing down in two important parameters of the logistic map, where a sudden population change happens. Deep learning-based approaches have been developed to address this issue, but they often fail to balance performance and computational efficiency. To understand how structural features influence the functionality of multiscale networks, researchers are turning to theoretical frameworks that link structure to function through dynamic models. Here, we explore how structural and functional relationships can be captured in a unified framework, where the network's structural model is directly connected to its functional model. We investigate this framework using a standard model known as the Kuramoto model, and we analyze the connection between the network's synchronization capabilities and the model's synchronization capabilities. We identify key factors that contribute to the synchronization capabilities, and we propose a method to quantify the impact of network structure on the synchronization capabilities. Our framework enables researchers to better understand the dynamic behavior of complex systems and identify the structural and dynamic relationships that govern their functionality.

In this task, each entry consists of multiple features, including both numerical and categorical data, and aims to produce an ordered list based on a relevance score for every possible combination. We demonstrate that current neural network approaches, using encoders, RNNs, or transformers, fail to effectively capture or generate ordered lists. In contrast, our proposed solution, a global ranking model, achieves better results. The model applies a projection to each feature, integrates the result using a separate sub-model for each entry feature type, and calculates a relevance score from the output. The model is optimized through a contrastive loss function and is specifically trained for ranking tasks. In experiments on three real-world datasets, our model outperforms baseline models in terms of ranking metrics. Notably, it achieves superior performance with significantly fewer parameters.

In contrast to datasets with detailed pixel-level annotations, there are numerous publicly available collections of patient data that are only lightly marked, if at all.  These datasets are valuable because they can help us train and evaluate medical image algorithms with minimal or no markers.  Our goal was to create a comprehensive directory of such public datasets, available online and accessible to everyone.  We focused on datasets that are routinely used in research and are available in standard formats. social networks has highlighted a key concept: criticality. This key notion is found in critical systems that exhibit sudden shifts in dynamics, often analyzed through a specific transition called a sudden synchronization transition. This transition happens when individual elements within a network come together to create unified clusters, altering the overall system's coherence. We have developed a comprehensive framework to analyze and control this synchronization transition using diverse network structures and individual elements. This framework has a wide range of applications, including understanding the human brain and complex social systems. Additionally, we have discovered a direct link between criticality and the synchronization transition, demonstrating that random binary networks can exhibit optimal criticality when they reach a synchronization threshold. Moreover, we have shown that precise control over criticality is possible by modifying diverse networks, such as random binary networks linked to functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) brain scans.

-density parity-check (LDPC) codes have historically centered on the capacity to decode a code that has been subjected to binary symmetric channel (BSC) and Gaussian channel interference. This research delves into the broader scope of generic channel conditions to ascertain the existence and characteristics of the LDPC ensemble's threshold. Our findings confirm the existence of such a threshold for almost all decodable codes, with the exception of those that lie in close proximity to the all-zero code rate. This result underscores the versatility and adaptability of LDPC codes, making them suitable for use in a broad spectrum of channel conditions. This discovery also facilitates the systematic study and comparison of LDPC codes across different ensemble configurations and decoder algorithms. This research is particularly useful in identifying promising candidate LDPC codes for standardization efforts. This work is an extension of a previously published study in 2019, which focused on specific channel conditions.

Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) in ecological studies, stemming from a lack of understanding regarding how to properly fit these models. This problem is compounded by a failure to apply fundamental principles of probability theory to the formulation of the likelihood function for GLMMs, leading to a significant issue in their application. Bayesian inference, however, offers a potential solution to this problem. Although the benefits of GLMMs over traditional linear mixed models are evident, there is a pressing need to rectify the flawed likelihood function used in these models. This research clarifies the probability theory behind GLMMs, rectifies their likelihood function, and demonstrates the correct application of both frequentist and Bayesian inference methods. Furthermore, the consequences of using an incorrect likelihood function in a GLMM are examined, along with the impact of applying a Bayesian approach.

Although various tools exist for optimizing and scheduling stream processing applications, fault-tolerant reconfiguration in the face of unexpected events such as sudden surges in throughput remains a significant challenge. In this research, we extend an existing stream processing compiler called PACT to support fault-tolerant reconfiguration in the face of such events. We introduce two reconfiguration strategies: 1) stream processing application reconfiguration to shift load from overloaded components to underutilized components, and 2) stream processing framework reconfiguration to add more components to handle increased throughput. We also introduce a novel type safety check that ensures the correctness of reconfiguration, and a cost function-driven optimization technique to minimize stream processing costs. We evaluate our work using both existing and self-written workloads, and our results show that our reconfiguration approach can significantly reduce latency and processing costs while handling sudden surges in throughput.

Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in processing natural language and have outperformed traditional rule-based approaches like the Frame-based Method (FBM). However, relying solely on FBMs with FB frames leads to a loss of contextual information, resulting in inaccurate sentence interpretations. In this study, we introduce a new frame consisting of three components: (1) a binary code representing the presence of specific words within the sentence, (2) a natural language interpretation of the sentence, and (3) a list of key words and their corresponding parts of speech. Each component of this new frame has a predetermined output, enabling frame-based accuracy while incorporating essential sentence context through the FB natural language. We assess the effectiveness of this new frame by training a model to generate binary codes from a dataset of Semeval 2014 Task 28, and then use an FB version of the T5 architecture to convert these natural language interpretations into binary codes. This two-step process results in a significant improvement in context precision over traditional FBM models.

In a PT-symmetric setting, we analyze a three-way waveguide network with equal-length input channels and demonstrate that only a specific combination of identical input signals results in a non-zero output signal when activated. We then explore the robustness of this property against perturbations and deviations from PT-symmetry, as well as in response to an asymmetric input configuration. We model a three-way waveguide network with equal input channel lengths using a 6-port unitary matrix and demonstrate that only a specific combination of PT-symmetric eigenmodes yields a non-zero output signal, providing insight into the underlying working principle of the device. We also derive an analytical expression for the beta parameter in PT-symmetric systems, which dictates the critical PT-symmetry breaking point and enable us to compare it with numerical simulations. We discover that, in this three-way waveguide network with equal input channel lengths, PT-symmetry does not guarantee the desired output signal, and that a particular input configuration is required to break this requirement. We find that, in this scenario, PT-symmetry provides a mechanism for signal switching, with a critical PT-symmetry breaking point that can be verified both numerically and experimentally through the derived $\beta$ parameter expression.

This investigation focuses on analyzing the system's stability by evaluating how many events in the relevance time window must occur in response to an initial perturbation. Our research highlights the system's tendency to reach a balanced state, where the correlation between events in the relevance time window balances out. This phenomenon is a manifestation of the ergodic property, where the network iterates through various states in response to different initial conditions. The time it takes for the system to achieve this equilibrium varies depending on the window's length and determines a time scale for perturbations to fade. This equilibrium is characterized by values that align with theoretical predictions for random matrices. Additionally, we analyze the distribution of events within the window, revealing the network's state to be a mix of ordered and random components. This mix influences the values observed within the window, which in turn affects the time it takes for the system to achieve ergodicity. Our findings underscore the ergodicity property as a key indicator of the phases within this system.

The aim is to select a set of edges that form a minimum power spanning tree with the lowest possible total weight. This problem is NP-hard for any power law exponent greater than 1, and it remains unclear whether a tree exists with a weight that grows sublinearly in relation to the worst-case exponentially large algorithmic bounds. To address this concern, we explore the common metric used for assessing color constancy performance, known as the Constant Correlation (CC) score, and determine its connection to color accuracy scores. Our research reveals that conventional color accuracy scores can yield misleadingly high scores when a model exhibits strong test-time overfitting, a critical concern given their widespread use in benchmarking. In response, we introduce a novel metric, called the Normalized Color Accuracy Score (NCAS), which normalizes color accuracy scores to account for both color accuracy and model overfitting tendencies, thereby preventing high scores solely due to overfitting tendencies. Our NCAS formulation reveals that the conventional CC score can be expressed as $\sqrt{1-k^2}$ times the NCAS, where $k$ denotes the conventional color accuracy score divided by its NCAS. Our research also reveals that in typical scenarios, NCAS and conventional color accuracy scores yield comparable rankings, thereby suggesting that conventional color accuracy scores can still provide useful benchmarks, albeit with the risk of not solely reflecting color accuracy. Our research also yields novel insights into the conventional CC score and its components, thereby contributing to the theoretical understanding of the CC score.

Although computational models of language have made significant advancements, they have often fallen short in capturing the full complexity of contextually informed linguistic behavior. In this research, we introduce a novel dataset, SocialMetaphor, which consists of 12,000 examples of students in Mexico adapting a metaphorical conversation by discussing race based on their familiarity with the speakers. This corpus serves as a diverse collection of linguistic contexts that we formulate as a multi-task contextual language modeling problem. Our experiments demonstrate that several advanced contextual language models can effectively predict a range of social variables, including dialect, gender, age, and familiarity, to some degree. Notably, we find that models are particularly successful in predicting familiarity, but struggle to accurately identify racial backgrounds. In our analysis, we also explore how different features, including speech style, sentence length, and punctuation, can provide some insight into a speaker's racial and demographic backgrounds.

Freeman and Schmitt in 1999, which indicated an anomalous drop in schlieren intensity near the ionization front in a gradually ionized gas, can be explained by the phenomenon of ion-neutral ponderomotive force, first proposed by Shklovskii in 1957. modern cryptography, termed "power leakage," which occurs when an encryption algorithm's power consumption is influenced by its plaintext or ciphertext. Inspired by this concept, we developed a destructive algorithm, known as the Power Attack, capable of revealing a secret key despite limitations on how much power is leaked. Unlike traditional side-channel attacks that assume independent power leakages, this algorithm accounts for the interdependence of leakage models, which is essential in modeling side-channels like DPA and DFA. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the majority of symmetric encryption schemes, including AES, Serpent, and Camellia, are vulnerable to the Power Attack under realistic leakage scenarios. We formally defined and characterized the Independence Power Leakage Model, and provided an analytical framework for assessing the independence of leakage. This framework forms the foundation for the Power Attack, which we also make available to the public.

To address this concern, researchers have been working on developing explainable AI (XAI) tools to provide more interpretable insights into the predictions made by these models. This issue is exemplified by the problem of subgraph model discovery, where the goal is to identify the appropriate statistical model for observed, independently and identically distributed, graph-valued observations. Existing research typically focuses on binary observations and offers various hypothesis testing procedures to distinguish between a specific null hypothesis and a range of alternative hypotheses. In contrast, our work takes a more agile approach by aiming to identify the optimal parametric model from a given finite set of possible models. This general framework has numerous practical applications, including a specific problem where sensors monitor a network of hosts for malicious activity and must determine the most likely type of attack from a predefined set. Our solution involves developing and evaluating two procedures for learning the optimal model, which are then compared through extensive computer simulations.

This approach can be implemented in free space by measuring the intensity in opposite directions using two photodetectors and taking the difference between them. A more efficient method of achieving the same result can be done in integrated photonic platforms, where on-chip on-off beam splitters and interferometers are used. We demonstrate that polaritonic systems inherently exhibit a significant difference in emission intensity when guided by a waveguide versus a broad space, resulting in at least 90% purity. However, this difference is often difficult to measure due to the varying nature of the background light. By employing the differential measurement concept, we show that we can obtain values as high as 99.9% with just two photodetectors. Moreover, we identify scenarios where the emission exhibits non-classical behavior under both measurement conditions.

metal vapor has long served as a valuable research tool in quantum physics.  The research community now possesses complete knowledge of the fluctuations in light scattering from hot vapor under the influence of inhomogeneous broadening.  In this study, we present a way to restore the quadratic relationship between light scattering intensity and atomic fluctuations in an otherwise transparent frequency range of the alkali metal D1 line.  By combining two laser beams with opposite detunings from the resonance, we demonstrate that scattered light fluctuations follow a squared law in low temperature cesium vapor cells. Additionally, by using rubidium, we show that this scattering can also be observed in warmer vapor clouds.

We propose using "interaction-free measurement" to create multi-qubit entanglement without direct interaction between the qubits, only through their interaction with light fields. This approach results in a multi-qubit state that's not only highly entangled but also robust against photon loss, as long as they're directed at different qubits. We show that starting from any initial state, a single beam-splitter is enough to generate this robust entangled state, as long as we discard the case where both photons are detected. By fine-tuning the system, we can also obtain the dishched W state from this free-light interaction. We also explore how this free-light construction can be used to perform Hitting Time and Hamiltonian simulation more efficiently than traditional methods.

Telescope Array Project is to detect gravitational waves using gravitational lensing to map the sky and identify the sources of these waves. The array consists of 16 gravitational lens telescopes, each with a diameter of 12 meters, spaced 2000 meters apart, operating at frequencies between 50 Hz and 5 kHz. The proposed design for the array spans various frequency ranges, from 0.1 kHz to 5 kHz, and the best design proposed here covers the 0.1 kHz to 1 kHz frequency range, with a detection bandwidth of 0.05 kHz. The proposed array design enables the detection of approximately 1000 gravitational wave events, including 100 binary neutron star mergers, 1000 binary black hole mergers, and 5000 hybrid events. The array can also reconstruct gravitational wave waveforms, providing polarization information and range information, and can locate events with an accuracy of 1 square degree.

Unlike previous approaches, VIA goes beyond simply altering model updates to infer their underlying content through unique characteristics of IoT device-generated updates. This challenge is compounded by the presence of road users whose potential movements need to be predicted to avoid collisions. A key aspect of this prediction involves identifying potential obstacles that an autonomous vehicle may encounter while accelerating to reach its target speed. These future barriers are defined as the minimum distance another road user could cover in a given time frame, which is influenced by their current and anticipated acceleration. This research proposes a method to project these potential barriers into the state space, consisting of an autonomous vehicle's position and velocity. It is shown that the shape of these barriers is determined not only by their distance and speed but also by their possible obstacles in the state space, which is a discovery that could influence the design of control barriers certificates for obstacle-aware vehicles. Moreover, it is proposed that the distance to these barriers be measured in a weighted state space, taking into account an intersection's specific geometry.

Memory (LSTM) have gained significant popularity in handling sequential data, attributed to their exceptional sequential modeling capabilities. However, the widespread adoption of LSTMs is hindered by their intricate internal workings, which are not well-understood. This research delves into the inner workings of a single LSTM, aiming to shed light on its operational mechanisms. A key finding is the discovery of a persistent state that enables the transport of information across the sequence. Building on this, a metric has been developed to quantify the expressive capacity of the model by analyzing its ability to manipulate this persistent state. Through theoretical and practical experiments, a proposed claim is supported: under certain conditions, a single-layer LSTM can effectively learn complex temporal patterns. Additionally, a proposed optimization for reducing redundant state storage is demonstrated to be successful. Ultimately, a significant contribution is made to the field of deep temporal understanding by providing a foundational framework for comprehending the behavior of a single LSTM.

The field of Syntax-Based NLP (SyB-NLP) focuses on exploring NLP from the perspective of human language structure, analyzing sentence components and their relationships. Although SyB-NLP methods have been applied to various tasks like Dependency Parsing and Coreference Resolution, they often involve replacing neural components with rule-based or greedy approaches, without reevaluating the underlying data representation. CFCR divides coreference resolution into two tasks: coarser-grain coreference cluster formation and finer-grain coreference cluster refinement. Experimental results on the OntoNotes 5.0 dataset show that the proposed CFCR method outperforms the current state-of-the-art, achieving a higher F1 score of 77.9, and outperforming the baseline by 3.3 points, while also surpassing the best semi-supervised neural method on the dataset.

Utilizing data from the UV spectrometer and the magnetometer, a study has been conducted to examine the relationship between Saturn's rotation and the phases of its year, particularly during the northern hemisphere's summer solstice. The study found that the period of the planet's rotation is linked to the phase of its year, with this relationship being affected by the amount of sunlight the planet receives. As the northern hemisphere entered deeper into its summer, the period of the planet's rotation became disconnected from the year's phase, with the Hubble Space Telescope observing an irregular pattern of the planet's rotation.

A commonly used solution to address this issue is the application of regularization techniques. In this study, we investigate the mathematical foundations of the combined backpropagation and regularization method. By leveraging the Kullback-Leibler divergence to measure the difference between the trained network and a pre-defined network, we can understand the regularized network as a variational approximation of a probabilistic model of data. settlement as an inherently safe process is a misleading notion that needs to be debunked. Despite being enshrined in the GSCC and DCGS legal frameworks, this definition is not universally applicable, especially not in the context of the banking system as a whole. The safe nature of bilateral netting does not guarantee the safety of multilateral clearing processes, and the vice versa also applies. Furthermore, the equivalence of multilateral netting and sequential bilateral netting is a fallacy. Although settlement finality is an essential component of a safe process, it does not encompass the entire concept of safety. Furthermore, even with the adoption of a fully collateralized and thus theoretically safe clearing process, banks could still face a catastrophic loss of money due to a systemic failure of reference assets, such as what happened during the 2008 financial crisis with mortgage-backed securities.

MacPherson introduced a groundbreaking concept of a virtual fundamental class within the context of moduli spaces that contain singularities. Building upon this foundation, our research develops new properties of this class in the homology of the Grassmannian space. By carefully defining an underlying geometric structure for the spaces defined by |a, b>, we identify conditions under which a non-trivial geometric homology class arises. Specifically, we find that a non-trivial class arises when a, b are both greater than or equal to 2n plus 2, where n is a positive integer. Additionally, we find that this non-trivial class generates a substantial portion of the homology of the Grassmannian, accounting for all but the initial few homology groups.

The analysis focuses on the time development of an electron under the Schrödinger equation, within a potential well. The electron distribution is defined as a product of two identical, orthogonal spatial wave functions, resulting in four possible frequency spectrum components. As the frequency differences decrease, the discrete structure of the spectrum becomes negligible, mimicking a continuous spectrum. The four possible combinations of the wave functions are represented by a two-level quantum system, with its properties controlled by altering the frequency spectrum. The probability of finding the electron in either excited or ground states over time is determined, with increased discrete resolution leading to more pronounced quantum beating. Simulations show that an approximately 1 fs period can be achieved through appropriate selection of the spatial wave functions. The implications of these findings for electron dynamics research in nanostructures are discussed.

We establish that when information is encoded in d-dimensional systems, both classical and quantum information can be efficiently protected with a qubit-like overhead, provided the encoding systems are relatively prime. Specifically, we demonstrate that a significant threshold exists where noisy qudit channels can be effectively corrected with a code rate approaching one using concatenated Bacon-Shor codes. To achieve this, we develop a universal quantum error correction scheme that utilizes only qudit gates and measurements, is locally implementable, and minimizes the threshold to approximately $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2}$, depending on the qudit dimension. By leveraging the flexibility of qudit operations, we show that increasing the dimension can lead to substantially smaller overheads, even when errors are limited to Pauli-type errors.

Although recent studies have applied the full ERG in various contexts, they remain limited in number. We develop a general framework that enables the exploration of how a system evolves under different ERG flow types, and we illustrate our approach by investigating two distinct flow types: the Wilsonian flow and the Gross-Neveu flow. Our framework allows us to compare and contrast the effects of different flow types, and we utilize it to analyze the role of the flow type in determining fixed points, as well as investigate how the choice of flow type affects the stability of an interesting non-Gaussian meta-stable state. Our results reveal that the flow type has a significant impact on the location of the relevant fixed point, and that the meta-stable state exhibits distinct behavior depending on the flow type chosen. Our study provides valuable insights for future applications of the full ERG, and our framework may be applicable to a wide range of such investigations.

We introduce the concept of strong recurrence, providing sufficient conditions for certain groups to be strongly recurrent or non-recurrent. For instance, we show that certain random walks on the general linear group $GL_d(\mathbb{Z}^d)$ are non-recurrent. Conversely, we prove that certain random walks on the symmetric group $S_d$ are strongly recurrent for large generators, a result that also implies $IRW_d$ and $CRW_d$ are recurrent. We establish a connection between recurrence and the topological transitivity of underlying shift spaces. This underlying space's entropy is linked to the Drift of the random walk, leading to a non-recurrence proof for $GL_d(\mathbb{Z}^d)$ and implying recurrence for $IRW_d$ and $CRW_d$.

This difficulty arises when calculating the entropy of a system reversed by simply doing so. When the number of microstates representing the reversed entropy is not equivalent to that of the original system, this task becomes impossible using traditional methods. We present a solution to this problem for systems that lose or gain information during the reversal process. This solution involves analyzing the work performed on or by the system as it undergoes expansion or contraction. Key examples include erasing a bit of information and resetting a system to its initial state. In these cases, we find that the work performed aligns with established nonequilibrium thermodynamic identities, resulting in an irreversible entropy change equal to the information lost or divided by a constant. Furthermore, we discuss how to interpret the direction of work performed on or by the system in relation to its reversed counterpart.

AR at the Max-Planck-Institut für Plasmaphysik in Germany provides detailed diagnostics for detailed analysis of detailed interactions between ICRF and plasma. These include determination of power deposition profiles, dispersion of ICRF waves, and wave scattering. This paper presents the results of an investigation into electron cyclotron bounce resonances and the associated resonant heating effects. It shows that these were clearly observed in the experiment for off-axis discharges using both circularly and linearly polarized ICRF waves at a frequency of 245 MHz. A shift in the resonance position and an increase in width with decreasing major radius were found to agree with theoretical predictions. A significant deposition of power at the bounce resonance was confirmed by power profile measurements, as well as by simulations. A ring-like pattern of plasma density at the resonance location was observed through diagnostics, indicating a region of resonant heating. This pattern disappeared when the ICRF was switched off. Furthermore, the ring-like pattern persisted across the blob even with co-currently polarized ICRF waves, suggesting that the observed resonant heating was not due to wave-current interactions. A detailed comparison of simulations and plasma density observations supports electron cyclotron bounce resonant heating as the primary mechanism of plasma heating at the resonance location.

This study aims to assess the efficacy of a biopesticide, Bacillus thuringiensis, in controlling the diamondback moth, an invasive and destructive pest of cruciferous plants. A laboratory experiment was conducted to determine the optimal concentration of biopesticide that would result in maximum mortality rates of adult diamondback moths across three life stages: eggs, larvae, and pupae. A range of concentrations (1x10^5, 1x10^6, 1x10^7, 1x10^8, and 1x10^9 CFU/mL) were applied to each life stage, and the life stages were maintained for seven days to monitor the effects of the treatment. The findings of this study have the potential to inform future research and diamondback moth management strategies.

our research proposes a new version, called the retrograde Cheshire cat effect, where an object appears to move backward while a part of it remains stationary. This study delves into the consequences of non-response in systematic sampling by examining various forms of induced selection effects through the lens of the inclusion probability concept. Different non-response models are contrasted, and it's discovered that the Bernoulli model, which treats the probability of a response as independent of the sampled element, is the only one that accurately represents a simple random sample. On the other hand, it's shown that other non-response models, including those that are step-function based or linearly proportional, induce correlated data sets that require the use of more complex analysis methods. , the gauge-fixing process results in four constraints that limit the available degrees of freedom, effectively restricting the gauge symmetry. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through an example involving smooth functions, which was successfully simulated with minimal dispersion and spurious oscillations. The method's versatility is further highlighted by its application to more complex problems, including problems with discontinuous coefficients and problems defined on moving domains with irregular boundaries.

While advancements in deep learning have significantly improved speech-to-text transcription and machine translation, they've also led to post-editing being bypassed. Our research introduces a novel deep learning-based model, named ST2WT, capable of directly converting spoken language to written language across different languages. The ST2WT architecture combines the features of an encoder-decoder and copy mechanisms, with an attention-based encoder and a two-stage decoder that selectively generates text or copies words. The ST2WT model was evaluated using the Switchboard corpus, with a subset of 11 English post-editing terms added to the original 450 French target vocabulary. The model achieved an accuracy of 71.8% in the Switchboard test set, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models, including direct speech-to-text translation and speech-to-text transcription models.

By comparing our results to those from mean field theories, we discover that strong on-site interactions cause a phase transition from a charge density wave to a uniform particle distribution as the hopping energy increases relative to the electron-electron interaction strength.  Next-nearest-neighbor hopping alone induces a finite order parameter in the random phase approximation, which is significantly overestimated when considering two-particle correlations.  Although strong on-site interactions generally suppress superconductivity, in this small cluster, they enhance d-wave pairing due to kinetic energy gain from virtual hopping processes.  This increase is consistent with findings in larger systems without next-nearest-neighbor hopping.  However, adding next-nearest-neighbor hopping results in a substantial rise in V_0, an order parameter representing the ground state density matrix fluctuation, particularly when starting from a d-wave paired state.  This significant growth in V_0 may pose a serious challenge to traditional methods of evaluating order parameters using two-body correlation matrices.
